html:
The Pazyryk carpet is the oldest known pile carpet in the world, woven around the 4th century BCE. It was found in 1949 in a frozen burial mound in the Altai Mountains of Siberia.

The Soviet archaeologist Sergei Rudenko dug the Pazyryk burials, tombs of horse riding nomads related to the Scythians. Water had seeped into the tombs and frozen, so wood, felt, cloth and even tattooed skin survived. The carpet lay in mound number five.

It is about two metres square, with around 36 knots in every square centimetre, as fine as many modern carpets. Its centre has a grid of star shaped patterns. Around it run borders of deer and of men on horseback or leading horses.

Where it was made is debated. Its style is close to the art of Achaemenid Persia, and many think it was made in Persia or Armenia and traded or given to the nomads. It shows how far goods moved across the steppe long before the Silk Road. It is now in the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg.
sum: The Pazyryk carpet is the oldest known pile carpet in the world, woven around the 4th century BCE. It was found in 1949 in a frozen burial mound in the Altai Mountains of Siberia.
